It’s completely understandable why that feels like a contradiction. When we hear "one" and "three" in the same sentence, our brains naturally want to do math—and in math, 1+1+1 equals 3, not 1.

However, in Christian theology, the Trinity isn't seen as a mathematical problem, but as a description of God's nature. Here is a breakdown of how theologians explain this concept:

### Essence vs. Person
The distinction often used to explain this is the difference between **essence** and **person**:
*   **Essence (What God is):** This refers to God's "being" or "substance." Christians believe there is only one divine essence or one "being" that is God. As one source notes, "Essence means the same thing as 'being'... since God is only one essence, He is only one being, not three" (Cru, [Understanding the Trinity](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).
*   **Person (Who God is):** While there is only one "being," that one Being exists eternally as three distinct Persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit.

### Why It Isn't a Contradiction
The idea is that a contradiction would only exist if we said God is three in the *same way* that He is one. Because God is described as Spirit and exists outside the limitations of our three-dimensional universe, He can be infinitely more complex than we can fully grasp (EveryStudent, [What is the Holy Trinity?](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

To help visualize this (though every human illustration eventually falls short), people often use analogies:
*   **States of Matter:** Like water being liquid, ice, and steam—different forms, but the same substance (H2O) (EveryStudent, [What is the Holy Trinity?](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).
*   **Mathematics of Multiplication:** Rather than addition (1+1+1=3), some suggest thinking of it as multiplication: $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ (EveryStudent, [What is the Holy Trinity?](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

### The Relational Aspect
Beyond the mechanics, the Trinity is also about relationship. It suggests that God is inherently relational—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have loved and interacted with one another for all eternity.

It is okay to find this mystery difficult. Many theologians admit that while we can understand the core truths, the full depth of how an infinite God functions is something that human understanding may never fully map out.

It is true that there is a significant difference in how Christianity and Islam view Jesus. While Muslims view Jesus as a prophet, Christians believe that Jesus is more than just a prophet.

Here is how those views differ according to the sources provided:

*   **The Nature of Jesus:** While Muslims believe Jesus is a prophet but not "God in the flesh" (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html), Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the **Son of God** and the "living God" (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html).
*   **The Meaning of "Son of God":** Christian teaching often views Jesus' sonship not in a physical sense, but in a spiritual one. He is seen as God incarnate, who took on human form to be closer to humanity (EveryStudent — Slovak, https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame).
*   **The Crucifixion and Resurrection:** Another fundamental difference is that Muslims do not believe in the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html). For Christians, however, the death and resurrection of Jesus are fundamental truths of the faith (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html).

In short, while both faiths revere Jesus, Christianity sees Him as the fulfillment of God's long-standing plan to bring people back into a relationship with Him (EveryStudent — Slovak, https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame).

I hear the frustration in your question, and I want to be honest with you: there is no simple explanation that can take away the pain or make the suffering of a child feel okay. When people talk about this, it can often feel like they are trying to use logic to explain something that is deeply emotional and devastating.

While different people offer different perspectives, here are some ways that Christian thought has attempted to address this heavy question:

*   **The Reality of Free Will:** One perspective is that God gives human beings true freedom to make choices. This means that while God is good, humans are free to choose actions that are corrupt or evil. It is not God's fault when people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it through their own choices (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).
*   **A Broken World:** Another view is that suffering exists because we live in a world where sin is a reality. This has resulted in a world where things like disease, accidents, and tragedy occur (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).
*   **God's Presence in Pain:** Rather than offering a detached explanation, some point to the person of Jesus. The idea is that God did not stay distant from suffering, but entered into it by becoming human and experiencing suffering himself. This is seen as a way to show that he is with people in their pain (thelife, [https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).
*   **The Promise of Justice:** There is also the belief that while God allows people the freedom to act, there will ultimately be a time of divine justice where everyone will answer for what they have done (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).

These aren't meant to be "dodges" to dismiss your feelings, but rather different ways people try to reconcile the character of a good God with the very real presence of pain in our lives. If you are navigating this through personal grief or a deep sense of injustice, please know that your anger and questions are a natural response to a broken world.

It is completely understandable why that sounds like a contradiction. Many people feel the same way when they first encounter the concept. In Christian theology, this concept is called the **Trinity**, and while it is often considered a profound mystery that defies easy human logic, there is a specific way Christians explain it to avoid it being a contradiction.

The key distinction used to explain this is the difference between **essence** (what something is) and **person** (who someone is).

### 1. One Essence, Three Persons
According to [Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html), the doctrine of the Trinity means there is one God who exists eternally as three distinct Persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 
*   **Essence (Being):** This refers to *what* God is. God is one in essence, meaning there is only one divine "being" or "substance." He is not a collection of different "ingredients" that make up a deity, but one single being [Cru](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).
*   **Person (Identity):** This refers to *who* God is. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct Persons. They are not just different roles or "masks" that God wears; they are distinct enough that, for example, the Father can send the Son into the world [Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).

### 2. Why it isn't a contradiction
The idea is that a contradiction would only exist if Christians claimed God is "three" in the same way He is "one." Instead, the belief is that God is one in *essence* but three in *person* [Cru](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).

To help visualize this, people often use analogies, though theologians note that no human analogy is perfect:
*   **The Sun:** You have the star itself, the light it emits, and the heat it provides. They are distinct, yet they are all part of one sun [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html).
*   **Water:** It can exist as liquid, ice, or steam. While they look and act differently, they are all still $H_2O$ [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html).
*   **Math:** Some describe it not as $1+1+1=3$, but as $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html).

### 3. A Relational God
Ultimately, many Christians see the Trinity as a beautiful way to describe a God who is inherently relational. Because God is three Persons, He has existed in a perfect relationship of love, interaction, and joy for all eternity [Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

It's okay to find this confusing—many theologians suggest that because God is spirit and exists outside our three-dimensional understanding, His nature will always be a mystery to the human mind [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html).
